stories.title: Odisha evacuates over 59,000 as cyclone Arnab triggers widespread flooding

reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Odisha deployed 313 disaster response teams and evacuated 59,028 people as flooding in the aftermath of cyclone Arnab inundated homes, isolated villages and disrupted transport across nine districts, officials said on Thursday.
Rescue operations were concentrated in Ganjam and Gajapati, where heavy rainfall left settlements cut off and made some areas inaccessible to boats.
Authorities began airlifting stranded residents, with an Indian Coast Guard helicopter completing its first rescue sortie on Thursday afternoon.

State disaster management minister Suresh Pujari said nine National Disaster Response Force teams, 60 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force teams and 244 Fire Services teams were engaged in rescue operations.
Those evacuated included 3,001 pregnant women and 11,882 residents of Ganjam.
Ganjam accounted for the largest deployment, with 45 ODRAF teams and seven NDRF teams, followed by Gajapati, where 12 ODRAF teams and one NDRF team were operational, Pujari said.
Malkangiri, Koraput, Rayagada, Nabarangpur, Kalahandi, Nuapada and Kandhamal were also affected.
Chief secretary Anu Garg said floods had hit around 300 villages in Ganjam, leaving 70 marooned.
The state coordinated with the Union Home Ministry to arrange aerial rescues after rising water prevented disaster response personnel from reaching some locations.
The government had begun an operation to airlift 2,328 people from the 70 cut-off villages, Garg said.
Special Relief Commissioner Rajesh P Patil said further helicopter sorties were following the initial evacuation flight.
In neighbouring Gajapati, heavy rain and flash floods affected 711 villages.

stories.title: Adani makes new $3.3 bn EU gamble
stories.summary: Mumbai: Adani Ports and Special Economic Zones (APSEZ) has submitted a binding offer of $3.3 billion (euro 3 billion) for Evos Terminals, a pan-European liquid storage and terminals company, said people aware of the development. Gautam Adani’s flagship company is seeking a key role in consolidation of the sector, especially in the continent, amid geopolitical volatility and heightened concerns over energy security, they said, with the West Asia conflict having affected the group’s domestic port volumes.The five-year-old Evos is owned by Igneo Infrastructure Partners, a global asset manager, which in turn is held by First Sentier Group. It has eight tank terminals with a total storage capacity of 6.4 million cbm at seven key European ports in five countries making it strategic for global port operators and owners of maritime infrastructure assets. In 2025, it's EBITDA was estimated at 200 million euros.Its portfolio includes storage for motor fuels such as gasoline but also eco-friendly options such as bio-diesel, sustainable aviation turbine fuel, green naphtha, bio-ethanol, e-methanol and bio-marine fuels.Earlier this year, Igneo had mandated Morgan Stanley to run a formal sale process that had seen keen interest from several global contenders including KKR, EQT and other financial sponsors and specialised PE buyout groups such as Macquarie, Goldman Sachs Alternatives and BlackRock as well as pension funds including CPP Investments and operators like LBC Tank Terminals Chane and Exolum, among others.135337886APSEZ submitted the binding offer earlier this week as part of the competitive auction process, said the people cited. A final decision is expected in the coming weeks. Amsterdam-headquartered Evos completed a euro 950 million debt raise through its financing arm Evos Finance BV in July, refinancing much of its existing debt facilities. The liquid storage operator structured the deal as a mix of private placements and bank debt, securing an investment-grade rating in the process. Chief executive officer Harry Deans had said then that the exercise would help the company execute its strategy more effectively, citing opportunities to grow the business with customers as the energy transition continues.Adani’s overseas push comes after it lost a 10 billion pound pursuit of UK’s Associated British Ports (ABP) to super fund IFM last week. On Wednesday, the management said it was evaluating 20 assets, including ports and terminals, as part of global expansion plans.“Our strength is containers, so the first thing we look at is where opportunity is driven by containers,” APSEZ CEO Ashwani Gupta said on an earnings call. “We are also considering liquid terminals because ports tomorrow maybe a gateway to energy transition.”Global FootprintAPSEZ operates 15 ports and terminals in India, with four international facilities in Israel, Tanzania, Sri Lanka and Australia. It handles more than 140 types of liquid cargo. Its domestic cargo-handling capacity stands at 653 million metric tonnes, according to the company’s latest operational disclosures. The Adani Group’s marine platform, Astro Offshore, has contracted with Oceaneering International to strengthen its deepwater engineering and offshore execution capabilities in Europe. This marks APSEZ’s entry into specialised subsea operations in Europe, advancing its ambition to build one of the world’s largest marine platforms in the world.APSEZ, Evos and Igneo didn’t respond to queries.The Adani company’s overseas acquisition strategy is centred on identifying the right cargo mix and assessing an asset’s potential returns before committing capital. It had Rs 8,483 crore in cash and bank balances at the end of March, as per data compiled by ETIG.Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Adani was weighing a similar sized bid for another Dutch energy storage group VTTI as supply disruptions make such firms more valuable for energy trading and commodity traders.Energy SecurityThe Iran war and supply disruptions across the hydrocarbons and chemicals value chain has forced countries and companies to seriously evaluate energy storage and logistics. ET was the first to report on August 18 that Aegis Logistics was closing in on an $1.5 billion acquisition of Dubai-based Tristar Holdings and expanding the footprint of the oil and gas logistics company beyond domestic storage and distribution into international maritime transport, fuel distribution and aviation fuelling. The transaction was announced a fortnight back.Similarly, Singapore said it will begin storing Saudi Arabian oil from next year as it responds to global energy disruption due the war in the Gulf. The oil will be stored in the Jurong Rock Caverns, an underground facility on a man-made island off Singapore’s southern coast that can hold up to nine million barrels. Last month, a trio of European companies — Evos, SEFE and Petrogas E&P — signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore technical, operational and commercial partnerships across the carbon dioxide (CO₂) transport and storage value chain.The ports-to-data centre conglomerate already has a presence in Haifa in Israel and is aiming for a string-of-pearls strategy to connect its hubs in India, West Asia and Europe.“They want to create a corridor between Mundra in Gujarat and western Europe. This is becoming a strategic importance and an energy security issue for India,” said a UK-based commodity trader specialising in the space. “Currently, the company also has footprints spread out in Australia, Africa and Colombo, Sri Lanka… and (has) a mega global expansion plan.”In FY26, 12% of the company’s revenue and 6% of its consolidated ebitda came from its international ports business.APSEZ management also said the company is stepping up investment in India, raising its FY27 capital expenditure guidance to Rs 15,000-17,000 crore from Rs 12,000-14,000 crore earlier. It reported capital expenditure of Rs 10,521 crore in the first half of FY27. Gupta said the higher investment guidance was driven by accelerated projects in India and did not include any additional international capex, even for organic expansion.“With strong cash flows, a healthy cash balance and a net debt-to-ebitda ratio of 1.9x, APSEZ is well-positioned for further expansion. Capacity enhancements at key ports, ongoing infrastructure projects, and global port acquisitions provide visibility for stable growth in FY27 and beyond,” said Alok Deora, an analyst with Motilal Oswal.Its key assets in India — Mundra, Dhamra, Hazira and Vizhinjam — are among the ports where investments are being accelerated.“The increase in capex does not include any international capex, even organic,” Gupta had said. “This increase in capex is mainly in India.” The company has also raised its FY27 revenue guidance to Rs 44,000-46,000 crore and earnings before interest, taxes and amortisation (ebita) guidance to Rs 26,000-27,000 crore, increasing both expectations by Rs 1,000 crore each. stories.headline: Year 2026 resembles 1991, could be deemed as inflection point for Indian economy: Chief Economic Advisor
stories.title: Year 2026 resembles 1991, could be deemed as inflection point for Indian economy: Chief Economic Advisor
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 29: The year 2026 resembles 1991, and it could be deemed an inflection point for the Indian economy, which has been facing not only external challenges but also structural constraints in manufacturing, energy, agriculture and technology, Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran said on Thursday. Addressing the ISID-IDRA national conference, Nageswaran further said that, in the global context, India is a source of macroeconomic stability and resilience, which sometimes tend to get forgotten in the noisy world of social media narratives. “2026 resembles 1991, and many of you should not immediately think that when we talk about the word resemblance, it is not the same as identical. Identical means that you have the same balance of payments crisis. “No. The point is, it was an inflection point for us in 1991, and 2026 is also, or even 2025, could be deemed as inflection points for us,” he said. Nageswaran said that while the 1991 balance of crisis brought four decades of accumulated constraints to a head- a moment of reckoning more than a passing shock- the external stress of 2026 has brought India to a fork in its growth journey and invites a fundamental re-examination of strategy. “In 2026, the challenge is not only external. Structural constraints in manufacturing, energy, agriculture and technology add to the pressure,” he said. Nageswaran pointed out that the worst shocks now arrive not because of accidents of nature, but by design. “Just as last week, we saw China announcing an export licensing regime for tunnel boring machines and for many other products of infrastructure goods, which India will be needing,” he said. The CEA said the weaponised dependence ends up eroding the more they are used, that is true. “The more countries weaponise their supplies, they become less effective over time. But there is a period when they are binding, because other countries cannot ramp up production just like that,” he said. Nageswaran observed that the next 20-30 years will be different from the 40 years pre-pandemic and added that most of the shocks which we faced before the pandemic were largely demand deficiency shocks. “So central bankers and fiscal policy could just stimulate and try to get out of trouble, whether it is the 1987 stock market crash, 1990-91 savings and loan crisis, the East Asian crisis of 1997–98, 2001 tech bubble or the 2008 global financial crisis. “Every single crisis was met with a standard playbook of low interest rates, together with or without quantitative easing, and some fiscal stimulus as well,” he said. The CEA said it is easy to stimulate when you consider the problems as only a matter of demand deficiency, but when supply falls short, it is about real stuff. “And that is not easily engineered or designed by monetary or fiscal policy. And higher interest rates, you can raise rates sky-high and cool an overheated economy,” he said. Nageswaran said in the next 30 years, monetary policy will be much more difficult to execute in a world of supply shortages causing real economic disruptions, both to output and to inflation. “Fiscal policy, broad support, stimulating of the economy where animal spirits are weak; it is easy to stimulate them with fiscal stimulus,” he said.

Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said that from Varanasi and Nagpur to Lucknow, Prayagraj, and Patna, the people have clearly passed a “no-confidence motion against” the PM’s policies. “The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he’s sermonising others! Before counting Congress’s seats, I wish he’d also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS’s stronghold of Nagpur?” Ramesh said in his post in Hindi on X. “Modi, stop the trolling. Crores of families are reeling from back-breaking inflation, the youth are unemployed, and private investment has ground to a halt,” he said. Drop the arrogance and reflect on these issues, Ramesh said. “From Varanasi and Nagpur to Lucknow, Prayagraj, and Patna, the people have clearly passed a no-confidence motion against your policies,” the Congress leader said. The Congress on Wednesday had hit back at Prime Minister Modi over his taunt, saying that if the PM is so confident that EVMs have no bearing on election results, he should prove his confidence in the BJP’s electoral prowess through action, not rhetoric. The Congress said if the PM believes that EVMs have no bearing on the election results then he should commit to conducting all Lok Sabha and upcoming Vidhan Sabha elections by ballot paper, going forward. The opposition party’s assertion came after Prime Minister Modi taunted the Congress for its dismal show in the MLC elections despite the use of paper ballots, a key demand of opposition parties in their campaign against EVMs. The BJP and its NDA allies won 16 of the 28 seats in the legislative council elections held across four states as the Congress won one, while the Samajwadi Party emerged winner in five seats in Uttar Pradesh, including two in Varanasi.

stories.headline: As China Plugs The 450 Million Tonnes of CO₂ Emissions Avoided By its Clean-Tech Exports In 2026, Some Skepticism Warranted
stories.title: As China Plugs The 450 Million Tonnes of CO₂ Emissions Avoided By its Clean-Tech Exports In 2026, Some Skepticism Warranted
stories.summary: China's growing dominance of clean-energy manufacturing is delivering an increasingly measurable environmental dividend to the rest of the world. But behind the emissions reductions is a larger industrial story, one that suggests Beijing's ambitions in clean energy have always extended well beyond the fight against climate change. A new analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), estimates that Chinese exports of clean-energy technologies could help avoid approximately 450 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions outside China in 2026 . That is equivalent to Brazil's annual emissions from fossil-fuel consumption, and nearly 2% of emissions generated outside China. The estimate covers Chinese exports of solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles and batteries. It reflects the emissions these technologies are expected to displace in importing countries, after accounting for emissions generated during their manufacture in China. The findings underline how central Chinese manufacturing has become to the global energy transition. They also highlight an interesting contradiction: the world's largest carbon emitter is increasingly becoming one of the most important enablers of emissions reduction elsewhere. A clean-tech export engine gathering pace The scale of China's export expansion is becoming difficult to ignore. During the first nine months of 2026, Chinese exports of electric cars and heavy vehicles grew 61% year-on-year, while wind turbine shipments increased 45%. Battery exports rose 39%, and overseas sales of solar equipment were up 22%, according to CREA's analysis. The environment or global dominance? The impact is particularly pronounced in developing economies. CREA estimates that around 76% of the lifetime emissions avoided through Chinese clean-tech exports in 2026 will accrue in the Global South. South and Southeast Asia together account for approximately 52% of the total. This is hardly surprising. Many of these economies continue to depend heavily on coal and other fossil fuels for electricity generation. Every additional unit of solar or wind capacity therefore has the potential to displace a relatively carbon-intensive source of power. Solar remains the largest contributor to the estimated emissions savings, reflecting both the sheer volume of Chinese solar exports and the favourable economics of deploying panels in high-irradiation markets. The analysis estimates that clean-tech exports made in 2026 could avoid around 8.4 billion tonnes of CO₂ over their operating lifetimes. For perspective, that is comparable to the combined annual fossil-fuel emissions of the United States and India. There is, however, an important qualification to these numbers. The 450-million-tonne figure is a projection based on export trends during the first three quarters of 2026, rather than a final audited full-year outcome. The lifetime emissions estimate also depends on assumptions about equipment operating lives, electricity generation, the fossil fuels displaced and the emissions intensity of manufacturing. Nevertheless, the direction and scale of the trend are significant. The Global South emerges as a major beneficiary One of the more interesting findings is the geographical distribution of the environmental benefits. South and Southeast Asia together account for more than half of the lifetime emissions savings attributed to China's clean-tech exports. India is identified as the largest national beneficiary in terms of avoided emissions, ahead of the United States. This is an important consideration for developing economies that face the twin challenges of rising energy demand and expensive fossil-fuel imports. Access to competitively priced solar modules, batteries and electric vehicles can help these countries accelerate electrification and reduce their exposure to volatile international energy markets. The recent disruption to oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has reinforced the case for alternatives, particularly in import-dependent Asian economies. Chinese clean-tech exports to Southeast Asia reportedly rose nearly 160% in the first nine months of 2026, according to figures cited in the analysis. For many countries, the attraction is straightforward: cheaper renewable energy equipment offers a route to greater energy security without waiting for domestic manufacturing capabilities to mature. Yet this growing dependence also raises a question that is becoming increasingly difficult to avoid: what happens when the countries supplying the technology also control the most important parts of its manufacturing and upstream supply chains? The other side of China's green energy story There is another side to China's growing contribution to global decarbonisation, one that deserves consideration before the country's clean-energy exports are celebrated as an unqualified environmental success. History suggests that environmental benefits may have been as much a useful justification for China's clean-energy ambitions as they were the primary motivation. Beneath the green narrative lay a much larger industrial ambition: to build manufacturing scale, create employment, develop globally competitive companies, secure export markets and establish control over technologies that would become indispensable to the world economy. The evolution of China's solar industry offers an instructive starting point. Research by Jonas Nahm of Johns Hopkins University has shown that the early development of China's solar manufacturing industry was driven substantially by export opportunities, entrepreneurial activity and investments by local governments. Central government intervention became more pronounced later, particularly as Beijing sought to address the consequences of rapid industrial expansion and build a stronger domestic market. The subsequent evolution of the electric vehicle industry offers an even clearer illustration of the convergence between industrial and environmental objectives. China's EV success has not been built on climate considerations alone. A combination of domestic market creation, policy support, manufacturing incentives, supply-chain integration and aggressive investment helped create an industry capable of competing globally. The result has been a manufacturing ecosystem spanning vehicles, batteries, critical materials and associated technologies. The economic significance is now considerable. A separate CREA analysis found that clean-energy industries contributed 11.4% of China's GDP in 2025 and accounted for more than a third of the country's economic growth. The sectors generated an estimated 15.4 trillion yuan, or around $2.1 trillion, in economic value. These numbers make it difficult to view China's clean-energy push simply through an environmental lens. It has also become a major economic growth strategy, providing manufacturing activity, investment opportunities, export revenues and employment across a vast industrial ecosystem. This is not to suggest that the environmental gains are artificial or that China's clean-energy policies have no climate rationale. Rather, the two objectives have reinforced each other. By building industries capable of producing clean technologies at enormous scale, China has created both a powerful domestic economic engine and an export proposition that other countries increasingly find difficult to ignore. From manufacturing dominance to geopolitical leverage The strategic implications of this industrial dominance have become clearer in recent years. China's restrictions on rare-earth exports in 2025 offered a particularly striking demonstration of how control over critical supply chains can be translated into geopolitical leverage. The restrictions covered additional rare-earth materials, processing technologies and magnet-related products, affecting industries ranging from electric vehicles and semiconductors to defence manufacturing. China accounts for more than 90% of global processed rare-earth production and magnet manufacturing, according to most informed estimates. The restrictions demonstrated that access to strategically important materials can become a negotiating instrument when Beijing considers it necessary. The lesson extends beyond rare earths. China occupies dominant positions across several clean-energy supply chains, including solar wafers and cells, battery materials and components, and electric vehicle manufacturing. For importing countries, this creates a complicated relationship. Chinese technology can make the energy transition cheaper and faster, but excessive dependence on a single manufacturing source can also create vulnerabilities. This is particularly relevant as governments in Europe, North America and elsewhere attempt to diversify supply chains through tariffs, local-content requirements and manufacturing incentives. Such measures may improve long-term industrial resilience, but they can also increase the cost of clean-energy deployment in the near term. There is a genuine dilemma here: how does the world reduce its dependence on Chinese manufacturing without making the energy transition more expensive and slower? The challenge for the rest of the world, including India For India, the implications are especially relevant. The country has made significant progress in building domestic solar module manufacturing capacity, with ambitions extending further upstream into cells, wafers and polysilicon. It is also seeking to establish a stronger domestic battery and electric vehicle ecosystem. However, China's experience demonstrates that manufacturing leadership is not achieved simply by announcing capacity or providing production incentives. It requires a combination of competitive costs, technological development, scale, integrated supply chains, access to capital and sustained domestic and international demand. India must therefore pursue two objectives simultaneously. It needs access to competitively priced clean-energy technologies to meet its own renewable energy ambitions, while continuing to build domestic manufacturing capabilities that reduce excessive dependence on imports. The same challenge applies to much of the developing world. Completely replacing Chinese supplies in the short term may be neither practical nor economically desirable. But building alternative manufacturing centres, diversifying sources of critical materials and developing regional supply chains will become increasingly important. There is also a broader lesson for policymakers. The success of China's clean-energy industries suggests that the transition can create economic opportunities on a scale that goes far beyond emissions reduction. Countries that approach it purely as an environmental obligation risk missing the industrial and employment opportunities that accompany it. An environmental dividend with an industrial price tag The estimated 450 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions that Chinese clean-tech exports could help avoid in 2026 is an impressive figure, and one that deserves recognition. The fact that much of the benefit is accruing in developing economies makes it particularly significant. But the story should not end there. China's clean-energy expansion has been driven by a combination of environmental objectives, industrial competitiveness, economic growth and strategic ambition. Its success in solar, batteries and electric vehicles has shown how these interests can converge to create industries that reshape global markets. The rare-earth episode, meanwhile, is a reminder that manufacturing dominance can also confer considerable geopolitical influence. For the rest of the world, the challenge is not to deny the environmental benefits of Chinese technology, nor to reject it simply because it comes from China. opening: China's growing dominance of clean-energy manufacturing is delivering an increasingly measurable environmental dividend to the rest of the world.
But behind the emissions reductions is a larger industrial story, one that suggests Beijing's ambitions in clean energy have always extended well beyond the fight against climate change.
body: A new analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), estimates that Chinese exports of clean-energy technologies could help avoid approximately 450 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions outside China in 2026.
That is equivalent to Brazil's annual emissions from fossil-fuel consumption, and nearly 2% of emissions generated outside China.
The estimate covers Chinese exports of solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles and batteries.
The findings underline how central Chinese manufacturing has become to the global energy transition.
They also highlight an interesting contradiction: the world's largest carbon emitter is increasingly becoming one of the most important enablers of emissions reduction elsewhere.
A clean-tech export engine gathering pace.
The scale of China's export expansion is becoming difficult to ignore.
During the first nine months of 2026, Chinese exports of electric cars and heavy vehicles grew 61% year-on-year, while wind turbine shipments increased 45%.
Battery exports rose 39%, and overseas sales of solar equipment were up 22%, according to CREA's analysis.
The environment or global dominance?
The impact is particularly pronounced in developing economies.
South and Southeast Asia together account for approximately 52% of the total.
This is hardly surprising.
Many of these economies continue to depend heavily on coal and other fossil fuels for electricity generation.
Every additional unit of solar or wind capacity therefore has the potential to displace a relatively carbon-intensive source of power.

Solar remains the largest contributor to the estimated emissions savings, reflecting both the sheer volume of Chinese solar exports and the favourable economics of deploying panels in high-irradiation markets.
The analysis estimates that clean-tech exports made in 2026 could avoid around 8.4 billion tonnes of CO₂ over their operating lifetimes.
For perspective, that is comparable to the combined annual fossil-fuel emissions of the United States and India.
There is, however, an important qualification to these numbers.
The 450-million-tonne figure is a projection based on export trends during the first three quarters of 2026, rather than a final audited full-year outcome.
The lifetime emissions estimate also depends on assumptions about equipment operating lives, electricity generation, the fossil fuels displaced and the emissions intensity of manufacturing.
Nevertheless, the direction and scale of the trend are significant.
The Global South emerges as a major beneficiary.
One of the more interesting findings is the geographical distribution of the environmental benefits.
South and Southeast Asia together account for more than half of the lifetime emissions savings attributed to China's clean-tech exports.
India is identified as the largest national beneficiary in terms of avoided emissions, ahead of the United States.
This is an important consideration for developing economies that face the twin challenges of rising energy demand and expensive fossil-fuel imports.
Access to competitively priced solar modules, batteries and electric vehicles can help these countries accelerate electrification and reduce their exposure to volatile international energy markets.
The recent disruption to oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has reinforced the case for alternatives, particularly in import-dependent Asian economies.
For many countries, the attraction is straightforward: cheaper renewable energy equipment offers a route to greater energy security without waiting for domestic manufacturing capabilities to mature.

Yet this growing dependence also raises a question that is becoming increasingly difficult to avoid: what happens when the countries supplying the technology also control the most important parts of its manufacturing and upstream supply chains?
The other side of China's green energy story.

There is another side to China's growing contribution to global decarbonisation, one that deserves consideration before the country's clean-energy exports are celebrated as an unqualified environmental success.
History suggests that environmental benefits may have been as much a useful justification for China's clean-energy ambitions as they were the primary motivation.

Beneath the green narrative lay a much larger industrial ambition: to build manufacturing scale, create employment, develop globally competitive companies, secure export markets and establish control over technologies that would become indispensable to the world economy.
The evolution of China's solar industry offers an instructive starting point.

Research by Jonas Nahm of Johns Hopkins University has shown that the early development of China's solar manufacturing industry was driven substantially by export opportunities, entrepreneurial activity and investments by local governments.
Central government intervention became more pronounced later, particularly as Beijing sought to address the consequences of rapid industrial expansion and build a stronger domestic market.
The subsequent evolution of the electric vehicle industry offers an even clearer illustration of the convergence between industrial and environmental objectives.
China's EV success has not been built on climate considerations alone.
A combination of domestic market creation, policy support, manufacturing incentives, supply-chain integration and aggressive investment helped create an industry capable of competing globally.
The result has been a manufacturing ecosystem spanning vehicles, batteries, critical materials and associated technologies.
The economic significance is now considerable.
A separate CREA analysis found that clean-energy industries contributed 11.4% of China's GDP in 2025 and accounted for more than a third of the country's economic growth.
The sectors generated an estimated 15.4 trillion yuan, or around $2.1 trillion, in economic value.
These numbers make it difficult to view China's clean-energy push simply through an environmental lens.
It has also become a major economic growth strategy, providing manufacturing activity, investment opportunities, export revenues and employment across a vast industrial ecosystem.
This is not to suggest that the environmental gains are artificial or that China's clean-energy policies have no climate rationale.
Rather, the two objectives have reinforced each other.

By building industries capable of producing clean technologies at enormous scale, China has created both a powerful domestic economic engine and an export proposition that other countries increasingly find difficult to ignore.
From manufacturing dominance to geopolitical leverage.
The strategic implications of this industrial dominance have become clearer in recent years.
China's restrictions on rare-earth exports in 2025 offered a particularly striking demonstration of how control over critical supply chains can be translated into geopolitical leverage.

The restrictions covered additional rare-earth materials, processing technologies and magnet-related products, affecting industries ranging from electric vehicles and semiconductors to defence manufacturing.
China accounts for more than 90% of global processed rare-earth production and magnet manufacturing, according to most informed estimates.
The restrictions demonstrated that access to strategically important materials can become a negotiating instrument when Beijing considers it necessary.
The lesson extends beyond rare earths.
China occupies dominant positions across several clean-energy supply chains, including solar wafers and cells, battery materials and components, and electric vehicle manufacturing.
For importing countries, this creates a complicated relationship.
Chinese technology can make the energy transition cheaper and faster, but excessive dependence on a single manufacturing source can also create vulnerabilities.
This is particularly relevant as governments in Europe, North America and elsewhere attempt to diversify supply chains through tariffs, local-content requirements and manufacturing incentives.
Such measures may improve long-term industrial resilience, but they can also increase the cost of clean-energy deployment in the near term.
There is a genuine dilemma here: how does the world reduce its dependence on Chinese manufacturing without making the energy transition more expensive and slower?
The challenge for the rest of the world, including India For India, the implications are especially relevant.
The country has made significant progress in building domestic solar module manufacturing capacity, with ambitions extending further upstream into cells, wafers and polysilicon.
It is also seeking to establish a stronger domestic battery and electric vehicle ecosystem.
However, China's experience demonstrates that manufacturing leadership is not achieved simply by announcing capacity or providing production incentives.
It requires a combination of competitive costs, technological development, scale, integrated supply chains, access to capital and sustained domestic and international demand.
India must therefore pursue two objectives simultaneously.

It needs access to competitively priced clean-energy technologies to meet its own renewable energy ambitions, while continuing to build domestic manufacturing capabilities that reduce excessive dependence on imports.
The same challenge applies to much of the developing world.
Completely replacing Chinese supplies in the short term may be neither practical nor economically desirable.
But building alternative manufacturing centres, diversifying sources of critical materials and developing regional supply chains will become increasingly important.
There is also a broader lesson for policymakers.
The success of China's clean-energy industries suggests that the transition can create economic opportunities on a scale that goes far beyond emissions reduction.
Countries that approach it purely as an environmental obligation risk missing the industrial and employment opportunities that accompany it.
An environmental dividend with an industrial price tag.
The estimated 450 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions that Chinese clean-tech exports could help avoid in 2026 is an impressive figure, and one that deserves recognition.
The fact that much of the benefit is accruing in developing economies makes it particularly significant.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday referred the long-running dispute between Reliance Industries Limited and the Government of India concerning the exploration and extraction of natural gas in the Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin to mediation.
The bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Baghchi and Justice V Mohana requested former Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai to act as the mediator.
It also requested her to take the assistance of two domain experts, to be suggested by the parties.
The Court noted that both sides had sought adjournments from time to time to explore the possibility of a settlement but had been unable to arrive at a viable solution.
Attorney General for India R Venkataramani and Senior Advocate Kapil Sibal informed the bench that the discussions did not reach a resolution.
"Both sides have requested adjournment from time to time to enable the parties to explore settlement.
We are informed that they themselves have not been able to find out a viable solution," the Court observed.
"In view of the request made on their behalf, we request Justice Ranjana P. Desai to act as the mediator.
We also request her to have the assistance of two domain experts as may be suggested by the parties," it added.

The dispute concerns allegations that Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) extracted natural gas that had migrated from an adjoining block operated by the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) into its own block in the Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin.
ONGC alleged that the gas reservoirs in the two blocks were interconnected, resulting in the migration of gas from its block into RIL's block.

Following a study by DeGolyer and MacNaughton, which indicated connectivity between the reservoirs, the Union Government constituted a committee headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice AP Shah to examine the issue.

stories.title: IMD update: Heavy rain may return to Coastal AP, TN, Kerala early next week
stories.summary: The India Meteorological Department has left the door open for intensification of the brewing depression into a deep depression that ranks only second to a cyclone in intensity
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A brewing depression over the Bay of Bengal could intensify as it races towards the Andhra Pradesh coast, raising the prospect of another spell of heavy to very heavy rain over the South Peninsula.

The system is expected to take shape by tomorrow (Saturday) and could strengthen further, bringing isolated very heavy rainfall of 11.5-20 cm to Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The rain belt is likely to lie south of the seas battered by very severe cycloneArnab just days ago.
It is not often that a very severe cyclone is followed so closely by another potentially powerful system.

Yet, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has left the door open for further intensification of the brewing depression, at least into a deep depression, the second-highest category in the hierarchy of low-pressure systems.
A combination of favourable oceanic and atmospheric conditions appears to support the possibility.
The emerging system could bring isolated heavy rain to Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal on Tuesday and Wednesday, besides Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam on Monday and Tuesday.
Kerala and Mahe, coastal Karnataka and South Interior Karnataka are also among regions forecast to receive heavy rain.
The wider rainfall outlook points to an extended spell of unsettled weather across the peninsula.
Isolated to scattered rainfall is forecast over Rayalaseema, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, and North Interior Karnataka for six days from Friday.
Kerala and Mahe, South Interior Karnataka, coastal Andhra Pradesh and Telangana could see similar activity for three days and again on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Lakshadweep is likely to receive such rainfall for three days from Monday, while coastal Karnataka comes under the spell on Saturday and Sunday.

stories.title: Telangana sends 2,000 staff, material to A.P. for power supply restoration work
stories.summary: Telangana dispatched nearly 2,000 staff along with emergency materials from its two distribution utilities to assist Andhra Pradesh in restoring power after the Arnab cyclone
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: The two distribution utilities of Telangana have dispatched emergency material along with nearly 2,000 staff to help restoration of power supply in the Arnab cyclone-hit areas in neighbouring Andhra Pradesh, following a request from that State.
Several power staff teams were sent to the cyclone-hit areas from Telangana on Tuesday along with some emergency material required for restoration of power supply.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and Energy Minister G. Ravi Kumar spoke to their Telangana counterparts.
A. Revanth Reddy and M. Bhatti Vikramarka, respectively, over phone on Tuesday and sought help in restoration of power supply.

It was explained that over 16,000 electric poles fell due to the cyclone in Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Srikakulam, Eluru, NTR, Guntur, Pravathipuram, Alluri Sitaramaraju, and a few other districts.
A.P. has the help of men and material from Telangana for the restoration work.

On getting instructions from Mr. Vikramarka the Chairmen and Managing Directors of TGSPDCL and TGNPDCL Jitesh V. Patil and K. Varun Reddy deputed the team from their Discoms to A.P. along with some material.
While SPDCL is sending over 1,300 of its staff, NPDCL is sending nearly 650 staff along with emergency response vehicles, battery-powered tree pruners and other equipment.
Deputy Chief Minister Mr. Vikramarka said the deputation of men and material to A.P. for the power supply restoration work was an indication of brotherhood between the two Telugu States.

While tariff hikes are very important for the telcos to boost revenues in India, Jio remains committed to be the most affordable player in the market.
